       3. FROM THE MARKETS   • This week brought AI investors to the brink, as Democrats’ midterm victories supercharged anxieties that had been building in the run-up to the vote. Thursday’s selloff erased $2.5 trillion in market value from the Nasdaq composite, pushing it into correction territory. Hedge funds dumped positions, while systematic trades amplified the losses.

Automakers around the world are focused on the U.S. because of Americans’ proclivity for large vehicles and SUVs, as well as their willingness to swallow record-high sticker prices. So what happened? As Sharon Terlep reports, China’s auto market faces a massive overcapacity crisis, and low-cost vehicles have conquered overseas markets and battered European automakers. Now, with rivals targeting the U.S., Detroit automakers are racing to maintain their high margins in the heartland.

This week’s Democratic victories are evidence that “the battered heart of American democracy is still beating,” writes Pulitzer Prize-winning biographer Jon Meacham. His essay for the Journal examines how the midterms have revived a tradition of democratic competition and what it means for the country’s future.

Trump Turns to a Hard-Line Adviser as His Political Challenges Mount
 
Plus, the U.S. is emerging as the last true profit engine for the world’s carmakers, and the reading list for the hottest class at Harvard
 
 
Stephen Miller, the White House’s new chief of staff. CHIP SOMODEVILLA/GETTY IMAGES
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

President Trump has responded to a stunning midterm defeat by elevating one of his most combative advisers.

 

Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump’s aggressive immigration policies, is replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. Wiles was seen as a moderating force on the president. Miller, by contrast, has long advocated a no-holds-barred approach to governing.

 

With Democrats taking control of Congress, Miller is expected to push for greater use of executive power and a confrontational response to congressional investigations. Our reporters explain why his appointment signals that Trump has little intention of changing course after the election.

 

And for a closer look at the man stepping into one of Washington’s most powerful jobs, here are five things to know about Miller.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• With Wiles’s departure, big business has lost a sympathetic ear in the White House.

 

• Vice President JD Vance and Gulf allies are pressing Trump to end the Iran war, but other advisers are making the case for renewed attacks.

 

• Elon Musk-run companies like SpaceX and Tesla have flourished in Texas thanks to white-glove treatment from elected officials. But that is about to change, Texas Democrats say.

 

• A dirty tricks campaign rattled Europe this week, leaving officials convinced a barrage of bomb threats and cyberattacks are coordinated. The thing they can’t figure out: Who’s behind it?

 

• The co-pilot in the Florida Learjet crash was 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras. Her dedication to flying in her teens wasn’t an anomaly, but part of a growing wave of young people getting an early start in their pilot careers.

 

• Jacked up by protein-heavy diet trends and a multitude of wellness fads, breakfast these days is increasingly likely to resemble its far heftier cousin: dinner.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• This week brought AI investors to the brink, as Democrats’ midterm victories supercharged anxieties that had been building in the run-up to the vote. Thursday’s selloff erased $2.5 trillion in market value from the Nasdaq composite, pushing it into correction territory. Hedge funds dumped positions, while systematic trades amplified the losses.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The U.S. is emerging as the last true profit engine for the world’s carmakers.

 

Volkswagen is considering making its first American pickup in 40 years, while Nissan is promising more rugged SUVs. Automakers around the world are focused on the U.S. because of Americans’ proclivity for large vehicles and SUVs, as well as their willingness to swallow record-high sticker prices. So what happened? As Sharon Terlep reports, China’s auto market faces a massive overcapacity crisis, and low-cost vehicles have conquered overseas markets and battered European automakers. Now, with rivals targeting the U.S., Detroit automakers are racing to maintain their high margins in the heartland.

 

5.

 

The midterms have given new life to an enduring American tradition.

 

For generations, Franklin D. Roosevelt and Ronald Reagan shaped American politics with visions that were different in detail but harmonious in principle. Both understood that a big, complicated, disputatious country requires negotiation, nuance and a willingness to live with less than what you want. This week’s Democratic victories are evidence that “the battered heart of American democracy is still beating,” writes Pulitzer Prize-winning biographer Jon Meacham. His essay for the Journal examines how the midterms have revived a tradition of democratic competition and what it means for the country’s future.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Democrats broke the 2028 map wide open.

 

The wave election that gave Democrats control of Congress and a majority of governors’ offices is creating another big benefit for the party: new pathways to the White House in 2028. Democratic victories in Texas, Ohio and Iowa have scrambled early thinking about how to garner the 270 Electoral College votes needed to win. The party also won governor’s races in all six familiar presidential swing states. Here’s a look at the expanded battleground and the new electoral math.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND

 

• Saturday: New Zealand is counting votes in its general election. Berkshire Hathaway reports earnings.

 

• Sunday: Israel’s president has said he will task a candidate with forming the country’s next government following last month’s election. Formula One’s São Paulo Grand Prix takes place in Brazil. Nascar crowns its Cup Series champion. The NFL holds a regular-season game in Madrid, with the Cincinnati Bengals facing the Atlanta Falcons.

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
46 square miles
 

That is how much territory Russian forces have gained in Ukraine this year through the end of October, compared with 1,874 square miles in 2025, according to the Institute for the Study of War. For the past two months, Russian forces have lost more land than they gained as Ukraine’s midrange strikes have pummeled supply routes behind the front lines with a variety of drones. We mapped out how Russia is failing on the battlefield.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Here’s the reading list for the hottest class at Harvard.

 

After our recent article about the surge in popularity of a humanities course for Harvard freshmen, readers asked us for the syllabus. And we’re happy to oblige. Here’s the reading list for the 2026-27 school year, along with the full list of assignments from previous years. The selections range from Homer’s “The Odyssey” to James Baldwin’s “The Fire Next Time.” Consider this your invitation to take on a Harvard reading challenge of your own.
